title: Embeddings & vector similarity
scopeHtml: What an embedding is, similarity metrics, dimensions and truncation, bi-/cross-encoders, asymmetric prefixes, model choice, ANN basics, calibration, drift, geometry pathologies, multilingual/multimodal, and production scenarios.

notes.title: What an embedding is
notes.html:
The idea. An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of content (a word, sentence, paragraph, image, audio clip or code snippet) so that content with similar meaning has vectors that sit close together. A neural network learns the mapping during training: it is a coordinate system for meaning, not a hash and not a compression of the original text. You cannot reconstruct the text from the vector (although inversion attacks can recover surprisingly much, so treat embeddings of sensitive text as sensitive).

Where it comes from. Early word embeddings (word2vec, GloVe) gave each word one fixed vector, so "bank" (river) and "bank" (money) shared a vector. Modern contextual embeddings come from transformer encoders or from the hidden states of language models: the vector for a sentence depends on every word in it. Sentence-embedding models are trained with a contrastive objective: pull the vectors of matching pairs together (a question and its answer, a query and a clicked document, two paraphrases) and push non-matching pairs apart. The training signal is what decides what "similar" means, which is why a model trained on question-answer pairs retrieves answers well and one trained on paraphrases clusters duplicates well.

Dimensions and size. Typical sizes are 384, 768, 1024, 1536 and 3072 dimensions. More dimensions can encode finer distinctions but cost more storage and search time. Storage is simple arithmetic:

  • 1 million vectors × 1536 dimensions × 4 bytes (float32) = about 6.1 GB.
  • The same in float16 is 3 GB; in int8 it is 1.5 GB; with binary quantization (1 bit per dimension) it is about 190 MB.
  • Add 30 to 100 percent on top for the ANN index structure (HNSW graphs store neighbour lists).

Input limits. Every embedding model has a maximum input length (commonly 512 to 8192 tokens). Text beyond it is silently truncated by many libraries, so the tail of a long document contributes nothing to its vector. That is one reason documents are split into chunks before embedding. Chunks should also be about one idea long: a vector for a 5,000-token chapter is an average blur of many topics and matches nothing well.

Pooling. A transformer produces one vector per token; to get one vector per text the model pools them: mean pooling (average of all tokens), CLS pooling (use the special first token) or last-token pooling (decoder-based embedders). Using the wrong pooling at inference gives silently degraded vectors, so always follow the model card.

Multilingual and multimodal embeddings. Multilingual models place sentences from different languages in one shared space, so a Hindi question can retrieve an English passage (cross-lingual retrieval). Quality is uneven: high-resource languages perform better than low-resource ones, and tokenization inflation (see the tokenization notes) also shortens the effective max length for those languages. Multimodal models (CLIP-style) map images and text into the same space, so a text query can retrieve images and vice versa. Always test on your languages and content.

Real life. A map. Cities that are culturally or geographically similar sit near each other. The reference "52.5 N, 13.4 E" is an embedding of Berlin; nobody reads the numbers, people only compare distances. A bad map (poor model) puts neighbouring cities far apart, and a map with too few dimensions (a 1-D line) squashes Paris and Rome together.

Tech. Keyword search finds documents that share words with the query. Embedding search finds documents that share meaning: "cheap flights" matches "budget airfare" even with no common word. It also fails in a different way: it can return text that is topically similar but does not actually answer the question, and it can miss exact tokens like an error code.

Worked example. Three sentences: A "How do I reset my password?", B "I forgot my login credentials", C "Best pizza near me". Embed all three; the cosine similarity of A and B is high (about 0.7 to 0.85), A and C is low (about 0.1 to 0.2). The exact numbers depend on the model, which is why you never hard-code a similarity threshold without calibrating it (see the thresholds section).

Common mistakes.

  • Embedding raw HTML or boilerplate (navigation, footers) so the vector is dominated by noise.
  • Mixing vectors from two different models in one index.
  • Forgetting to apply the model's required query/document prefixes.
  • Assuming the vector "contains" all the details of a long text.

Interview angle. Be ready to explain what training objective makes two texts close, why dimensionality is a cost trade-off, and why you chunk before embedding.

notes.title: Similarity: cosine, dot product and L2
notes.html:
The three measures. Given vectors a and b:

  • Dot product: a · b = Σ aᵢbᵢ. Large when the vectors point the same way and are long.
  • Cosine similarity: (a · b) / (|a| |b|). The dot product of the unit-length versions; it ranges from −1 to 1 and ignores length, only the angle matters.
  • Euclidean (L2) distance: |a − b|. Smaller means closer.

How they relate. If every vector is normalized to length 1, then |a − b|² = 2 − 2(a · b). So cosine, dot product and L2 produce the same ranking. Most modern text embedding models output normalized vectors (or are trained for cosine), so on those the choice is mostly about speed: dot product on normalized vectors is the cheapest and matches cosine exactly.

When length carries meaning. Some models (and some recommendation systems) let the vector length encode confidence or popularity. There, dot product intentionally favours long vectors, and cosine would throw that information away. This is why you follow the metric the model was trained with.

Worked example. a = (3, 4), b = (6, 8): they point the same direction. Dot = 18 + 32 = 50. Cosine = 50 / (5 × 10) = 1.0. L2 distance = |(−3, −4)| = 5. Cosine says "identical direction", L2 says "not identical", because L2 is sensitive to length. Normalize both to length 1 first and L2 becomes 0.

import numpy as np
def cosine(a, b): return a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b))
a = np.array([3., 4.]); b = np.array([6., 8.])
print(cosine(a, b))                      # 1.0
print(np.linalg.norm(a - b))             # 5.0
an, bn = a/np.linalg.norm(a), b/np.linalg.norm(b)
print(np.linalg.norm(an - bn))           # 0.0

Caveats of cosine.

  • Anisotropy. Embeddings from many models occupy a narrow cone of the space, so even unrelated texts can have cosine 0.5 or more. Absolute scores are not meaningful; only relative ranking within one model is.
  • Hubness. In high dimensions a few vectors become "hubs": they appear in the nearest-neighbour lists of a large share of queries regardless of relevance. Symptoms: the same irrelevant document keeps appearing. Fixes include re-ranking, normalizing against local neighbourhoods, or removing boilerplate documents.
  • Scores are not probabilities. 0.8 means different things in different models and for different query types.
  • Comparisons across models are invalid. You can only compare vectors produced by the same model and version.

Real life. Two people pointing at a landmark. Cosine asks whether they point the same way; dot product also rewards how far each arm is stretched; L2 asks how far apart their fingertips are.

Interview angle. Expect "when are cosine and dot product the same?" (normalized vectors) and "why did my top result change after I stopped normalizing?" (length now influences the dot product).

notes.title: Bi-encoders, cross-encoders and Matryoshka
notes.html:
Bi-encoder. Query and document are encoded separately into vectors, then compared with a cheap similarity. Document vectors are computed once, offline, and stored in an index. At query time you embed only the query and run nearest-neighbour search. Cost per query is tiny, so bi-encoders power first-stage retrieval over millions of items. The limitation: query and document never "see" each other during encoding, so subtle interactions (negation, exact conditions, numeric constraints) are lost.

Cross-encoder. Query and document are fed together into one transformer that outputs a single relevance score. Because every query-document pair needs a fresh forward pass, scoring a million documents per query is impossible. Cross-encoders are used for re-ranking the top 20 to 200 candidates from a bi-encoder, where their much higher accuracy is worth the latency (typically tens to a few hundred milliseconds).

Late-interaction models (ColBERT-style). A middle path: keep one vector per token, compare queries and documents token-by-token with a MaxSim operation. Accuracy near cross-encoders, efficiency near bi-encoders, at the price of much larger indexes.

Real life. A bi-encoder is skimming CV headlines to build a shortlist; a cross-encoder is interviewing each shortlisted candidate.

Asymmetric embeddings and prefixes. Queries are short and question-shaped; documents are long and statement-shaped. Many models are trained with different roles and expect a prefix such as query: and passage: (or an instruction string). Forgetting the prefix, or applying the document prefix to queries, quietly lowers recall without raising any error. Symmetric tasks (finding duplicates) use the same treatment for both sides.

Matryoshka representation learning. Normal embeddings spread information evenly across all dimensions, so chopping off the tail destroys them. A Matryoshka-trained model is optimized so that the first k dimensions (for several k: 64, 128, 256, 512...) are themselves good embeddings. You can store 256 of 1024 dimensions for 4x less memory and faster search with a small quality drop, or use a short vector for coarse retrieval then the full vector to re-score the candidates ("funnel" retrieval). Rules: only truncate models trained this way, and re-normalize after truncation.

Binary and scalar quantization. Independent of Matryoshka, you can store vectors as int8 (4x smaller) or 1-bit (32x smaller) and re-score the top candidates with the full-precision vectors. Combining Matryoshka truncation with quantization can cut storage 50x or more with careful evaluation.

Interview angle. Why two stages? Because accuracy and cost trade off: cheap model over everything, expensive model over a handful.

notes.title: Choosing an embedding model
notes.html:
Criteria that matter.

  1. Quality on your data. Public leaderboards (MTEB) are a starting point, not an answer: they average over tasks you may not have.
  2. Language and domain coverage. Legal, medical, code and low-resource languages often need specific models.
  3. Max input length and chunk size fit.
  4. Dimensions and storage/latency cost.
  5. Price and rate limits (API) or GPU/CPU footprint (self-hosted).
  6. Licence and data policy (can you send customer data to the vendor? is the model licence commercial-friendly?).
  7. Stability. API models can be deprecated; a change forces a full re-index.

How to decide. Build a small labelled retrieval set from real queries (50 to 200 queries, each with the documents that should be returned). Embed with 2 to 4 candidates, compute recall@k and nDCG, compare cost and latency, then choose. Re-run the comparison when your content or languages change.

Fine-tuning embeddings. When off-the-shelf models underperform on a narrow domain, fine-tune with in-domain (query, positive document, hard negative) triples. Hard negatives (documents that look relevant but are not) give the biggest gains. Evaluate for regressions on general queries.

Real life. Trying on shoes in your size rather than buying the best-rated pair online.

Common mistakes. Choosing the top MTEB model without testing; ignoring the licence; not budgeting the re-indexing work.

notes.title: ANN indexes
notes.html:
Why approximate. Exact nearest-neighbour search compares the query with every vector: O(N × d). For 10 million 1024-d vectors that is about 10¹⁰ multiply-adds per query, too slow for interactive use. Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a small amount of recall (maybe 95 to 99 percent of the true top-k) for 100 to 1000x speed.

Main index families.

  • Flat (brute force). Exact. Fine up to ~100k vectors or when you need perfect recall (and for evaluating ANN recall).
  • IVF (inverted file). Cluster the vectors with k-means into nlist cells; at query time search only the nprobe nearest cells. Low memory, easy to combine with compression (IVF-PQ). Recall depends on nprobe: higher is slower but better.
  • HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world). A multi-layer graph; search starts at the sparse top layer and greedily hops to closer neighbours, descending to denser layers. Excellent recall/speed trade-off, no training step, but high memory (graph links) and slower inserts/deletes. Key parameters: M (links per node), efConstruction (build quality), efSearch (query-time breadth).
  • PQ (product quantization). Split each vector into sub-vectors and replace each by a small code from a codebook. Compresses 32x or more with some recall loss; typically combined with IVF and with a re-scoring step.
  • DiskANN / disk-based graphs. For indexes larger than RAM.

Filtering. Real queries have filters (tenant_id = 7 AND language = "en"). Three strategies: post-filter (search, then filter: can return fewer than k results or none when the filter is selective), pre-filter (filter, then search a brute-force subset: slow for large subsets), and filtered ANN (the index supports filtering during traversal: best, but recall can drop on very selective filters). Always measure recall with your real filters, not only unfiltered.

Operations. Updates and deletes: HNSW handles deletes as tombstones and needs periodic rebuilds; IVF needs re-training when the data distribution drifts. Plan for incremental indexing, backups and rebuild time. Sharding by tenant or hash lets you scale out; replicas give availability and read throughput.

Real life. Finding a restaurant: choose the right district first (IVF) or follow signposts that get you closer street by street (HNSW); you do not walk past every restaurant in the city.

Interview angle. "How do you tune recall vs latency?" (efSearch/nprobe), "why can filtered search return too few results?" (post-filtering), "HNSW vs IVF?" (memory, build time, recall).

notes.title: Thresholds and evaluation
notes.html:
Why fixed thresholds fail. "Return anything above 0.8 similarity" assumes scores mean the same thing everywhere. They do not: distributions differ by model, language, query length, and corpus. A threshold that works on short FAQ queries will be too strict or too lax on long natural-language questions.

Calibrating a threshold. Collect labelled pairs (query, document, relevant yes/no) from real traffic. Plot score distributions for relevant and irrelevant pairs, choose the cut-off that hits your required precision (support bots usually want high precision) or recall (compliance search wants high recall), and re-measure after every model, chunking or corpus change. Often a better design is relative: return the top-k always, but let the generator say "the context does not contain the answer", plus a reranker score threshold, which is better calibrated than raw cosine.

Evaluation metrics (retrieval only).

  • Recall@k: fraction of queries for which at least one (or all) relevant documents appear in the top k. The first metric to check; if recall@20 is low the generator cannot succeed.
  • Precision@k: fraction of the top k that are relevant.
  • MRR: mean of 1/rank of the first relevant result; rewards putting the right answer first.
  • nDCG@k: handles graded relevance and discounts lower ranks.
  • Hit rate / success@k for single-answer lookups.

Building the eval set. Sample real queries; have humans (or a strong model with human spot-checks) mark relevant documents; include hard cases (typos, acronyms, multi-intent, unanswerable). Synthetic queries generated from chunks are cheap but easier than real ones, so use them to extend, not replace, real data.

Evaluate retrieval separately from generation. If the final answer is wrong you need to know whether retrieval failed or the model misused good context.

Real life. A smoke-detector sensitivity dial: you set it from real false-alarm data, not from a number on the box.

notes.title: Drift and re-indexing
notes.html:
What drifts.

  • The embedding model or version changes (API provider updates it, you switch models).
  • Preprocessing changes (new chunking rules, new cleaning, different prefixes).
  • The corpus changes in character (new product lines, new languages).
  • The queries change (users start asking different things).

Vectors from different models live in different spaces, so mixing them gives meaningless similarity. Even a minor version bump can shift the space enough to lower recall.

Safe migration playbook (blue/green for indexes).

  1. Store model_name, model_version, chunker_version with each vector.
  2. Build a new index with the new model alongside the live one.
  3. Evaluate on the labelled retrieval set; compare recall, latency, cost.
  4. Shadow traffic or canary a small share of queries.
  5. Switch the alias; keep the old index for fast rollback.
  6. Retire it after a stable period.

Cost planning. Re-embedding N chunks costs N × tokens × price; for 50 million chunks of 500 tokens that is 25 billion tokens, a real budget line. Batch APIs and incremental updates help. Choosing an embedding vendor is therefore a long-term commitment.

Detecting drift. Monitor retrieval metrics on a fixed probe set, average top-1 similarity, the share of queries with no result above threshold, and user feedback signals. A sudden drop after a deploy points to a pipeline change; a slow decline suggests content or query drift.

Real life. A library that changes its catalogue system: old and new shelf codes cannot live in one catalogue, so you build the new catalogue next to the old one before you cut over.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
One paragraph. An embedding is a learned vector where distance means similarity of meaning. Models learn this with contrastive training; the dimension count, max input length, pooling and required query/document prefixes are properties of the model you must respect. Normalized vectors make cosine, dot product and L2 rank identically; raw scores are not probabilities, and cosine suffers from anisotropy and hubness.

Key points to remember.

  • Bi-encoder = fast first stage, vectors precomputed; cross-encoder = slow, accurate re-ranker; late interaction sits in between.
  • Matryoshka vectors can be truncated (and re-normalized) to save memory; quantization (int8, binary) saves more, usually with re-scoring.
  • Storage ≈ vectors × dims × bytes, plus index overhead (30 to 100 percent for HNSW).
  • ANN: HNSW (best recall/speed, memory heavy), IVF (cheap, tune nprobe), PQ (compression). Test recall with filters; post-filtering can return fewer than k results.
  • Choose models with a labelled eval on your own data; check language, length, licence and re-index cost.
  • Do not hard-code similarity thresholds; calibrate them and prefer rerank scores or "answer not in context" handling.
  • Evaluate retrieval separately: recall@k, MRR, nDCG.
  • Changing the model, version or preprocessing requires a full re-index; migrate with a parallel index and rollback.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Normalize and dot product equals cosine."
  • "Retrieve wide with a bi-encoder, re-rank narrow with a cross-encoder."
  • "If the right chunk is not in the top k, no prompt can save you."
  • "An embedding model is part of your data schema: changing it is a migration."

questions.promptHtml: What is an embedding, how does a text embedding model produce one, and what does "similar" mean in that space?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know embeddings are a learned, task-shaped representation and not a magic "meaning" vector. Everything downstream (RAG, dedup, clustering) rests on this.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An embedding is a fixed-size vector of floats that a neural network maps an input to, trained so inputs that should be treated as similar land close together. For text, an encoder transformer produces per-token vectors, which are pooled (mean or CLS) into one vector. "Similar" is defined by the training objective, usually a contrastive loss on query/relevant-passage pairs, so closeness means "would be judged relevant or paraphrastic", not "true" or "same topic" in an absolute sense.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principles: a model needs numbers, not strings. A tokenizer turns text into token IDs; an embedding layer inside any LLM maps each ID to a vector. A sentence/text embedding model is different: it runs the whole sequence through a transformer, pools the token outputs into one vector, and is trained so geometry encodes a notion of relatedness.

"refund policy" -> tokenizer -> [ids] -> transformer -> token vectors (n x d)
                                                    -> pooling (mean / CLS / last-token)
                                                    -> 1 vector (d,)   e.g. d = 1024

Training: contrastive learning with in-batch negatives. For a batch of (query, positive passage) pairs, the loss pulls each query toward its positive and pushes it from the other passages in the batch (InfoNCE). Hard negatives (passages that look relevant but are not) sharpen the boundary. So the space encodes whatever the training pairs encoded: retrieval relevance, paraphrase, NLI, etc.

Runtime: one forward pass per text, cost grows with token count, output size is fixed at d regardless of input length. Longer inputs are compressed into the same d numbers, so long chunks blur multiple topics into one point (the "averaging" problem). Decoder-LLM-based embedders typically pool the last token or use mean pooling; check the model card.

Consequences: (1) the space is only meaningful relative to one model: vectors from two models are not comparable, (2) similarity is a ranking signal, not a probability, (3) embeddings capture topical/semantic relatedness well but are weak at negation, numbers, exact identifiers, and rare entities.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
m = SentenceTransformer("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5")
a, b = m.encode(["How do I get a refund?", "Return policy for orders"], normalize_embeddings=True)
print(a.shape, float(a @ b))   # (384,), cosine because vectors are unit length

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the embedding "captures meaning" without naming the training objective.
  • Comparing vectors from different models or versions.
  • Assuming a long document gets a proportionally richer vector. Dimension is fixed.
  • Expecting exact-match behavior (SKUs, error codes) from dense vectors.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Token embedding layer vs sentence embedding model? → The first is a lookup table inside an LLM; the second is a full encoder trained for whole-text similarity.
  2. Why do we pool? → Need one fixed-size vector from n token vectors; mean pooling is common, CLS or last-token for some models.
  3. Why does negation break embeddings? → "Is covered" and "is not covered" share almost all tokens and topic; contrastive data rarely forces them apart, so they sit close. Rerank or use a cross-encoder when polarity matters.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "a vector representing meaning, use cosine." Senior: names the objective, says similarity is model- and task-specific, flags the failure classes (negation, identifiers, long chunks) and pairs dense retrieval with lexical/rerank.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A support search returned "cancel subscription" docs for "do not cancel my subscription" intents; polarity was invisible to the bi-encoder until a reranker was added.

questions.subtopic: Cosine vs dot product vs L2
questions.promptHtml: Cosine similarity, dot product, and Euclidean distance: how do they differ, and when do they give identical rankings?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Metric mismatch is one of the most common silent retrieval bugs. This separates people who have configured a vector DB from people who have only read about one.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dot product mixes angle and magnitude; cosine is dot product divided by both norms, so it is angle only; L2 measures straight-line distance. If vectors are unit-normalized, ||a-b||² = 2 - 2·cos(a,b) and cos = dot, so all three give the same ranking. If they are not normalized, they can disagree, and I must use the metric the model was trained with.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• dot(a,b) = Σ aᵢbᵢ = ||a||·||b||·cosθ
  • cos(a,b) = dot / (||a||·||b||)
  • L2²(a,b) = ||a||² + ||b||² - 2·dot(a,b)

With ||a|| = ||b|| = 1: L2² = 2 - 2·dot, so ranking by smaller L2 equals ranking by larger dot equals larger cosine. Monotone transforms preserve ranking, though the values differ, which matters for thresholds.

Worked example, a = (3,4), b = (6,8), c = (4,3):

  • dot(a,b)=50, dot(a,c)=24. Dot ranks b first (longer vector).
  • cos(a,b)=50/(5·10)=1.0, cos(a,c)=24/25=0.96. Cosine ranks b first too, as b is the same direction.
  • L2(a,b)=5, L2(a,c)=√2≈1.41. L2 ranks c first. Three metrics, two different winners.

When magnitude carries meaning (some recommender models, where norm encodes popularity), dot product is intentional. For most text embedding models, norm is noise and the model is trained on cosine/normalized dot. OpenAI's embedding docs state their vectors are normalized to length 1 and that cosine is recommended, with dot product giving identical rankings.

Runtime: normalized + inner-product index is the fastest path (one multiply-add per dim, SIMD friendly). Many vector DBs offer cosine, dot, l2; cosine usually normalizes internally.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
a, b, c = map(np.array, ([3., 4.], [6., 8.], [4., 3.]))
cos = lambda x, y: x @ y / (np.linalg.norm(x) * np.linalg.norm(y))
print(a @ b, a @ c)                                   # 50, 24 -> b
print(cos(a, b), cos(a, c))                           # 1.0, 0.96 -> b
print(np.linalg.norm(a-b), np.linalg.norm(a-c))       # 5.0, 1.414 -> c

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring an index dot while storing un-normalized vectors from a cosine-trained model.
  • Assuming "normalized" without checking np.linalg.norm on a sample (quantized or truncated vectors are not unit length).
  • Reusing a cosine threshold after switching to L2 or dot (values live on different scales).
  • Calling cosine "distance" (1-cos) a metric; it violates the triangle inequality.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Cosine on zero vectors? → Undefined (0/0); guard with epsilon or drop empty inputs.
  2. Why prefer cosine for text? → Norm correlates with text length or token frequency, not relevance.
  3. Does normalization change top-k? → For a fixed query, cosine vs dot can reorder docs if doc norms differ; that is exactly when the metric choice matters.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cosine ignores magnitude, use it for text." Senior: derives the L2/cosine identity, checks actual norms, matches the training metric, and notes thresholds do not transfer across metrics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team created a pgvector index with L2 ops on cosine-trained vectors that were not unit length; recall looked fine in demos but long documents with large norms were systematically demoted.

questions.promptHtml: What does embedding dimensionality control, and what are the trade-offs of 384 vs 1024 vs 3072 dimensions?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you reason about quality, storage, latency and cost together instead of "bigger is better".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Dimension is the capacity of the vector to separate items. More dims generally buy a little retrieval quality but cost linearly in memory, index build time, and distance compute. I measure recall on my own data at a few sizes and pick the knee of the curve; for large corpora the storage and RAM bill usually decides.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Memory math (float32 = 4 bytes/dim):

  • 1M vectors × 384d = 1.54 GB; × 1024d = 4.1 GB; × 3072d = 12.3 GB.
  • 50M vectors × 1536d = 50e6 × 1536 × 4 = 307 GB, before HNSW graph overhead (links per node, often tens of bytes to a few hundred, depends on M; verify per engine).

Compute: brute-force scoring is O(N·d); ANN reduces N visited but each distance is still O(d).

Quality: gains flatten. OpenAI's published numbers show text-embedding-3-small (1536d) at 62.3% MTEB and 3-large (3072d) at 64.6% on their docs page, so doubling dimension plus a bigger model bought ~2.3 points (their figures, verify current). Quality depends more on the model's training than raw dimension; a good 768d model beats a poor 3072d one.

Capacity argument: dimension limits how many distinct "top-k relevance" sets a single-vector embedding can represent (theoretical limits of embedding-based retrieval are an active research area; treat as verify).

Levers to cut cost without retraining: Matryoshka truncation (see Q005), int8/binary quantization (see Q008, Q019), PCA (needs fitting and re-indexing).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def index_gb(n, d, bytes_per=4): return n * d * bytes_per / 1e9
for d in (384, 1024, 3072):
    print(d, round(index_gb(10_000_000, d), 1), "GB for 10M")   # 15.4, 41.0, 122.9

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking the highest-dim model by default and discovering RAM cost at 50M vectors.
  • Forgetting index overhead and replicas when sizing.
  • Judging by MTEB average rather than recall@k on your corpus.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does halving dims halve latency? → Distance compute roughly yes; end-to-end less so (network, rerank, graph traversal dominate).
  2. Can you just chop the vector? → Only if the model was trained for it (Matryoshka), otherwise quality collapses.
  3. Where does quantization fit? → int8 gives 4x, binary 32x memory cut; typically paired with rescoring top candidates using full-precision vectors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "higher dimension is more accurate." Senior: computes the RAM bill, shows diminishing returns, evaluates on own data, and lists truncation/quantization as levers.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 3072d index across 80M chunks needed ~1 TB RAM with replicas; moving to a 1024d Matryoshka-trained model cut cost by ~3x with a recall@10 drop under 2 points on the internal eval.

questions.promptHtml: Explain bi-encoders versus cross-encoders. Why do we not just use a cross-encoder for search?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core retrieve-then-rerank architecture. Tests complexity reasoning.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bi-encoder embeds query and document independently, so documents are pre-computed and searched by vector math; it is fast but compresses each text into one vector. A cross-encoder feeds query and document together through the transformer, so tokens attend across both and it is more accurate, but it needs one forward pass per pair, which is infeasible over millions of docs. So I retrieve top-100 with a bi-encoder and rerank with a cross-encoder.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Bi-encoder:   q -> E -> vq        d -> E -> vd      score = vq . vd     (docs offline)
Cross-encoder: [CLS] q [SEP] d -> E -> scalar relevance                (per pair, online)

Cost: N docs, bi-encoder = 1 query encode + ANN lookup (sublinear in N). Cross-encoder over everything = N forward passes per query. At 1M docs and 5 ms per pair on GPU batch, that is ~83 minutes per query. Rerank top-100 instead: 100 pairs, ~0.5 s sequential, far less batched.

Why cross is more accurate: full token-level interaction (can see that "not" modifies "covered"), whereas the bi-encoder bottleneck is a single vector. Late-interaction models (ColBERT style) sit in between: per-token vectors with MaxSim, more storage, better accuracy than single-vector.

Rerank scores are not comparable across queries (usually logits); use them for ordering, calibrate if thresholding.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
ce = CrossEncoder("cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2")   # verify model choice for your domain
pairs = [(query, d) for d in candidates]       # candidates from ANN top-100
scores = ce.predict(pairs)
ranked = [d for _, d in sorted(zip(scores, candidates), reverse=True)]

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reranking too few candidates (recall ceiling set by stage 1) or too many (latency).
  • Cross-encoder max length truncation silently cutting the answer-bearing part of a chunk.
  • Treating cross-encoder scores as probabilities.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does recall get lost? → Stage 1; rerank cannot recover docs never retrieved.
  2. Why not distill the cross-encoder into the bi-encoder? → Often done; gains are partial because single-vector capacity remains the bottleneck.
  3. LLM as reranker? → Works (listwise/pointwise) but costs tokens and latency; evaluate against a trained cross-encoder (see the RAG chunk for pipeline detail).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cross-encoder is slower but better." Senior: quantifies pairs×latency, states the recall ceiling, mentions ColBERT-style middle ground and score-calibration caveats.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Adding a 100-candidate cross-encoder rerank lifted answer accuracy but added 180 ms p95; the team batched pairs and cut candidate count to 40 after measuring recall@40.

questions.promptHtml: What is Matryoshka representation learning, and what can go wrong when you truncate embeddings?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical cost lever that is easy to misuse.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Matryoshka training makes the first k dimensions of the vector a usable embedding on their own, by applying the loss at several prefix sizes (e.g. 64, 128, 256, ... full). So I can store a shorter prefix and trade a little quality for large memory savings. The trap: after truncating I must re-normalize, and I must only truncate models trained that way.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
MRL (Kusupati et al., arXiv 2205.13147, 2022) nests coarse-to-fine information: early dims carry the most important signal. The paper reports up to 14x smaller embeddings for ImageNet-1K at similar accuracy and up to 14x retrieval speedups (their vision results; text gains are model-specific, verify).

OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models expose a dimensions parameter and their docs say a 3-large vector shortened to 256 dims still beats ada-002 at 1536 on MTEB. Their docs also state that if you shorten manually you must normalize afterward.

Why renormalize: a prefix of a unit vector has norm < 1. Dot product on truncated, un-normalized vectors is biased by prefix norm; cosine is fine but only if your index computes it as cosine.

Common architecture: two-stage search. Index 256d prefixes for cheap candidate generation, rescore top-200 with full-dimension vectors kept on disk.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
def truncate(v, k):
    t = np.asarray(v)[..., :k]
    return t / np.linalg.norm(t, axis=-1, keepdims=True)   # renormalize

# API-side alternative (OpenAI): client.embeddings.create(model="text-embedding-3-large", input=txt, dimensions=256)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Truncating a non-Matryoshka model (e.g. slicing a plain 768d BERT-style embedder): quality drops sharply.
  • Skipping renormalization with a dot-product index.
  • Mixing truncated and full vectors in one index.
  • Not re-tuning similarity thresholds after truncation (score distribution shifts).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why do early dims hold more info? → The multi-size loss forces every prefix to be independently useful, so the model packs coarse signal first.
  2. Truncation vs PCA? → PCA is post-hoc and needs fitting data; MRL is baked into training.
  3. How to pick k? → Plot recall@k vs dimension on your eval set and choose the knee against the memory budget.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "you can cut dimensions to save space." Senior: knows it needs MRL training, renormalizes, retunes thresholds, and uses a truncated-then-rescore design.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team sliced a non-MRL model to 256d to fit a free-tier vector DB limit; recall@10 fell from 0.84 to 0.61 before they switched to an MRL-trained model.

questions.promptHtml: Why do some embedding models require "query:" and "passage:" prefixes or instructions, and what happens if you skip them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common source of silent quality loss.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Queries and documents are different text types: a query is short and expresses an information need, a passage is long and contains answers. Many models were trained asymmetrically with a prefix or instruction telling the encoder which role the text plays. If I skip or mix the prefixes, the model sees inputs off its training distribution and retrieval quality drops, usually without any error.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Examples from model cards I checked: multilingual-e5-large expects "query: " and "passage: " prefixes on every input, including non-English text; for asymmetric retrieval, use "query:" for queries and "passage:" for documents; omitting prefixes degrades performance. Its inputs are truncated at 512 tokens and the vector is 1024d. Other families use instruction strings or special query prompts (BGE, Nomic, Instructor-style); the exact strings differ per model and version, so read the card (verify).

Mechanism: the prefix is just tokens, so the transformer conditions on it during pooling; training taught it to place "query:" vectors near "passage:" vectors that answer them. Symmetric tasks (duplicate detection, clustering) use the same prefix on both sides.

Runtime impact: prefix tokens count against max length and cost; embedding an index with the wrong prefix means re-embedding everything to fix.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
m = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-large")
docs = m.encode([f"passage: {t}" for t in chunks], normalize_embeddings=True)
q = m.encode(["query: how do I reset my password"], normalize_embeddings=True)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Indexing documents with the query prefix (or none), querying with the right one.
  • Applying the prefix on only one pipeline (batch indexer vs online service).
  • Copying prefixes from a different model.
  • Forgetting prefix tokens when budgeting max length.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you detect missing prefixes? → Golden-query eval: recall drop; compare embeddings of same text with/without prefix (cosine well below 1).
  2. Is HyDE related? → Different: HyDE generates a hypothetical answer to embed in the document space.
  3. Symmetric vs asymmetric tasks? → Dedup/similarity uses one role on both sides; retrieval uses query vs passage roles.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "add the prefix the docs say." Senior: explains training reason, centralizes the prefix in one shared embedding wrapper, versions it with the index, and adds a regression eval.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An online service added "query:" but the nightly indexer job did not add "passage:"; offline eval used a library helper that did, so it passed while production recall sagged.

questions.promptHtml: How do you choose an embedding model for a production search feature?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you select by evidence on your data and constraints, not by leaderboard rank.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I list hard constraints first: language coverage, max input tokens, dimension/storage budget, latency, license, and hosted vs self-hosted. Then I build a small labeled eval set from real queries (100-300 with relevant docs), shortlist 3-4 models, and compare recall@k and MRR on my corpus. MTEB gets me the shortlist; my own data picks the winner.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Axes:

Axis Why it matters
Domain Legal/code/medical text shifts vocabulary; general models may underperform
Languages English-only models degrade on other languages; check the model card's language list
Max tokens multilingual-e5-large truncates at 512 tokens; OpenAI v3 models accept 8,192 (per their docs). Truncated tails are never searchable
Dimension Storage and RAM (see Q003)
Training format Needs prefixes? Matryoshka?
Ops API rate limits and price vs GPU hosting; data-privacy rules
License Weights license may limit commercial use

MTEB is an average over many tasks; your task may be one narrow slice, and models can be tuned toward public benchmarks, so a +1 point average gap is noise for your workload.

Procedure: 1) sample real queries, 2) label relevant docs (LLM-assisted labeling plus human spot check), 3) compute recall@10/MRR/nDCG per candidate, 4) add latency and cost per 1M tokens, 5) choose with a decision table, 6) keep the eval as the regression gate for any future swap (see Q011).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def recall_at_k(ranked_ids, relevant_ids, k=10):
    return len(set(ranked_ids[:k]) & set(relevant_ids)) / max(1, len(relevant_ids))

for name, embed in candidates.items():          # embed(texts, role) -> normalized np.ndarray
    D = embed(corpus, "passage"); Q = embed(queries, "query")
    top = (Q @ D.T).argsort(axis=1)[:, ::-1][:, :10]
    print(name, sum(recall_at_k(t, rel[i]) for i, t in enumerate(top)) / len(top))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Picking the MTEB #1 model with a 512-token cap for 2,000-token chunks.
  • Evaluating on synthetic queries that mirror the chunk text (inflated scores).
  • Ignoring p95 embedding latency for query-time encoding.
  • Not budgeting for re-embedding when the vendor retires a model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Fine-tune or switch? → Switch first; fine-tune when you have thousands of in-domain pairs and a gap persists (see the fine-tuning chunk).
  2. Hosted API vs self-host? → Volume, privacy, latency, and operational burden; break-even math at your token volume.
  3. How to avoid lock-in? → Store raw text, version the model ID with the index, keep a migration path (Q011).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "top of MTEB." Senior: constraint table plus own-data eval plus total cost and migration risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team picked a leading general model, then found legal contracts with defined-term abbreviations retrieved poorly; a domain-tuned smaller model beat it by 9 points recall@10 on their labeled set.

questions.promptHtml: Explain at a conceptual level how HNSW and IVF work and what trade-offs they make versus exact search.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: You will configure vector DBs; tuning needs the mental model.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Exact search compares the query to every vector, O(N·d). ANN trades a bit of recall for sublinear time. HNSW builds a layered proximity graph and greedily walks from sparse top layers down to dense bottom ones. IVF clusters vectors with k-means and searches only the nearest few clusters. HNSW gives high recall and low latency but uses lots of RAM; IVF (often with product quantization) is leaner but needs training and tuning nprobe.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HNSW (Malkov and Yashunin, arXiv 1603.09320): each element is assigned a max layer with exponentially decaying probability; search enters at the top layer, greedily moves to the nearest neighbor, drops a layer, repeats, and at layer 0 explores with a candidate list of size ef. Typical knobs (names vary by engine, verify): M (links per node), efConstruction (build quality), efSearch (query breadth). Higher ef = higher recall, slower. Complexity is roughly logarithmic in N.

layer 2:  o--------------o                 (few nodes, long links)
layer 1:  o----o-----o---o----o
layer 0:  o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o-o          (all nodes, short links)
query: enter top -> greedy descend -> beam search at layer 0 (ef candidates)

IVF: k-means into nlist cells; query finds the nprobe nearest centroids and scans only those cells. Recall misses vectors whose true neighbor sits in an unprobed cell (boundary effect). IVF-PQ compresses vectors into short codes (e.g. 16-64 bytes) for large memory savings with approximation error.

Operational points: deletions and updates are awkward in graphs (tombstones, rebuilds); filtered search can hurt recall if the filter removes most graph neighbors (see Q021); index builds are CPU heavy; always measure recall against brute-force on a sample.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import faiss, numpy as np
d = 768; xb = np.random.rand(100_000, d).astype("float32"); faiss.normalize_L2(xb)
hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT)  # M=32
hnsw.hnsw.efConstruction = 200; hnsw.add(xb); hnsw.hnsw.efSearch = 64
flat = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d); flat.add(xb)
q = xb[:100]; _, a = hnsw.search(q, 10); _, t = flat.search(q, 10)
print(np.mean([len(set(a[i]) & set(t[i])) / 10 for i in range(100)]))   # recall@10 vs exact

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Defaults left untouched and recall never measured.
  • Using an HNSW index with the wrong metric flag.
  • Ignoring RAM for graph links on top of raw vectors.
  • Benchmarking on tiny data where brute force wins.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is exact search right? → Under roughly hundreds of thousands of vectors or when filters make candidate sets small.
  2. Why does recall drop with filters? → Graph traversal visits neighbors that the filter discards, leaving too few survivors.
  3. What does PQ lose? → Distance precision; fix by rescoring the shortlist with full vectors.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "HNSW is fast ANN." Senior: describes layers, ef/M trade-offs, memory, update/delete behavior, filter interaction, and measures recall vs brute force.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Raising efSearch from 16 to 100 recovered 7 points of recall@10 at +4 ms p95, cheaper than a bigger model.

questions.contextHtml:
A semantic search service uses a self-hosted embedding model whose card says "trained with cosine similarity; outputs not normalized." Index code:

import faiss, numpy as np
d = 1024
vecs = model.encode(chunks)                    # float32, shape (2_000_000, 1024), NOT normalized
index = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)                   # inner product
index.add(vecs)
q = model.encode([user_query])
scores, ids = index.search(q, 10)

After launch, users complain that long boilerplate-heavy chunks (legal footers, tables of contents) keep outranking the right answer. Offline eval in a notebook (which used sklearn.metrics.pairwise.cosine_similarity) shows recall@10 = 0.82; the live system measures 0.64 on the same queries. Mean vector norm in the index is 11.8 with std 4.1. QPS is 150; p95 is fine.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug, explain why only live metrics suffer, and fix it without downtime.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Retrain or switch models" or "tune top-k / add a reranker". It treats the symptom, never compares the notebook and the service code paths, and misses that the two used different metrics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the notebook metric the same as the index metric? (Notebook used cosine, index uses raw IP.) Does the model card say outputs are normalized? Are scores ever logged so I can correlate score with chunk length? Did the failing queries share a pattern (long docs)? Is there a replica I can rebuild into?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Normalize the query and keep the index as is only if I also normalize docs; the fast stopgap is a rerank-by-cosine step on the top-200 returned by IP, computed from stored vectors, which removes the norm bias at small cost. Not perfect (recall ceiling) but cheap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) metric mismatch: IP rewards large norms; (b) chunking differences between notebook and prod; (c) stale index vs fresh eval corpus; (d) missing prefixes (check card); (e) ANN settings (ruled out: it is a Flat index).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compute np.corrcoef(norms, rank_gain); recompute top-10 for 200 queries with cosine vs IP and diff; check overlap. Log ||v|| for the winning docs: expected high norms. Run the notebook against the prod index export to prove the metric is the only delta.
  5. Root cause: Inner product = ||q||·||d||·cosθ. For a fixed query, doc score scales with ||d||, so high-norm chunks get a bonus independent of relevance. The notebook used cosine so it never saw this.
  6. Fix: Short-term: normalize in both paths. Long-term: one shared embed() wrapper that always L2-normalizes and asserts unit norm.
def embed(texts):
    v = model.encode(texts).astype("float32")
    faiss.normalize_L2(v)                           # in-place
    return v
assert abs(np.linalg.norm(embed(["x"])[0]) - 1) < 1e-3

Rollout: build a new index from stored raw vectors (normalize in place, no re-embedding needed), shadow-query both, compare recall, swap alias. 7. Prevention: Unit test that asserts norm ≈ 1 on indexed and query vectors; CI eval using the production search function, not a notebook reimplementation; alert on mean-norm drift. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just retrain or change top-k; I would not re-embed 2M chunks (vectors are reusable, normalization is a pure transform); I would not keep the stopgap rerank after the real fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Model card says outputs are already normalized, yet norms vary → Then something else changed them: quantization, truncation, or a different model path; check whether you stripped a normalize layer.
  • You must keep dot product (norm carries popularity signal) → Then it is intentional; evaluate with and without, and use a documented metric choice, not an accident.
  • 20 B vectors? → Normalize at ingest, never at query.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A search team's offline eval ran through a notebook helper, while production used a raw inner-product index. Two sprints went into reranker tuning before someone diffed the two score paths.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests changing models or top-k; no root cause.
  • Hire: Spots IP vs cosine, normalizes, fixes the eval path.
  • Strong hire: Derives the norm bias, proposes no-re-embed rollout with shadow comparison, adds norm assertions and shared embed wrapper.

questions.promptHtml: Can you set a cosine similarity threshold of 0.8 to decide "relevant"? How do you pick and maintain thresholds?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Thresholds appear in dedup, "no answer" gating, and cache hits; naive values cause incidents.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No, cosine values are not probabilities and their distribution depends on the model, the metric, text length, and the domain. 0.8 might be near-duplicate in one model and "barely related" in another. I pick thresholds empirically: label pairs, plot score distributions of relevant vs irrelevant, choose a cutoff for the precision/recall trade-off the product needs, and re-check whenever the model changes.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Each model has its own score range due to anisotropy (Q013): some models put random unrelated texts at 0.6-0.7 cosine, others near 0.1. A fixed global number is meaningless across models.

Procedure:

  1. Sample N query-doc pairs, including hard negatives (topically close but wrong).
  2. Label relevant or not.
  3. Compute score distributions; choose threshold by target precision (e.g. P ≥ 0.95 for auto-answers) or by F-beta.
  4. Per-query relative signals can beat absolute thresholds: gap between top-1 and top-2, or score relative to the corpus mean.
  5. For gating ("answer from context or refuse"), combine with a reranker score or an LLM judge.
count
  |   ###                 irrelevant     ##
  | ######                           #########  relevant
  +------------------------------------------------ cosine
        0.45   ^cutoff 0.62     0.78

Overlap area is the unavoidable error. Thresholds should be per use case (dedup wants high, recall-first retrieval wants low).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve
p, r, th = precision_recall_curve(labels, scores)      # labels in {0,1}
import numpy as np
cut = th[np.argmax(p[:-1] >= 0.95)]                     # lowest threshold with precision >= 0.95

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding 0.8 copied from a blog.
  • Calibrating on easy negatives only.
  • Not re-calibrating after a model/version/truncation change.
  • Using one threshold across languages (score ranges differ by language).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is there a "probability" version? → Fit Platt/isotonic regression on labeled scores to map cosine to P(relevant) for one model.
  2. Semantic cache threshold risks? → False hits return wrong cached answers; need high precision and per-intent validation.
  3. Why do scores shift with chunk length? → Longer text pooled to the same vector tends to look closer to generic content; monitor by length bucket.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "0.8 works well." Senior: treats thresholds as calibrated, model-specific config with an eval, bucketed by language/length, and under monitoring.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A semantic cache at threshold 0.9 returned an answer for "cancel by Friday" to "cancel after Friday"; adding a rerank/verification step plus a stricter threshold removed the wrong hits.

questions.promptHtml: What is embedding drift, and how do you handle changing or upgrading an embedding model with a live index?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Vectors from different models live in different spaces; mishandling this is a classic outage.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: There is no mapping between two models' spaces, so a new model means re-embedding the entire corpus and re-indexing, then switching queries to the new model atomically. I run it blue/green: build the new index alongside, shadow-evaluate on a golden set, switch an alias, keep the old index for rollback. "Drift" also covers silent changes: provider updates behind the same name, preprocessing changes, and data distribution shift.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Types:

  1. Model change (planned): incompatible spaces. Query vector from model B against doc vectors from model A returns garbage (cosine can still be a plausible-looking number).
  2. Silent API change: provider updates weights under a floating alias; pin versioned model IDs when offered, and store model ID + date in metadata (verify provider versioning policy).
  3. Pipeline drift: tokenizer or chunker change, new prefix, new normalization.
  4. Data drift: new vocabulary (product names, slang) the model never saw.

Migration plan:

1. Freeze eval set + metrics (recall@k, MRR, p95)
2. Re-embed corpus into index_v2 (batch, rate-limited, resumable; store raw text + chunk IDs)
3. Dual-write new documents to v1 and v2 during backfill
4. Shadow queries: embed with both models, compare results + eval
5. Cut over via alias / feature flag, canary 5% -> 100%
6. Keep v1 for rollback window; then delete

Cost: tokens × price. 100M chunks × 300 tokens = 30B tokens; at an illustrative $0.02 per 1M tokens that is $600 for the API call alone (check current prices), plus compute and index build time. Self-hosted: GPU hours.

Trade-off alternatives: query-time adapters trained to map old to new space (research-y, lossy); hybrid search that tolerates temporary quality loss. Normally just re-embed.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Per-doc metadata makes mixed-model states detectable.
record = {"id": cid, "text": text, "vec": vec.tolist(),
          "embed_model": "provider/model@2025-01", "prefix_v": 2, "chunker_v": 3}
# Query service refuses to search an index whose embed_model != the configured query model.
assert index_meta["embed_model"] == CONFIG["embed_model"], "model/index mismatch"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Upgrading the query path before the index finished (or vice versa).
  • Not storing raw text, so re-embedding needs a re-crawl.
  • Mixed vectors from two models in one index during a partial backfill.
  • No rollback plan.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to detect drift without labels? → Monitor score distributions (top-1 mean, margin), click-through, zero-result rate, canary queries with known answers.
  2. Can you map old vectors to new? → Learned linear adapters exist but are lossy; not for critical paths.
  3. How do you throttle a 30B-token backfill? → Queue with rate limits, batch size tuning, idempotent chunk IDs, checkpointing.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "re-embed everything." Senior: blue/green with shadowing, dual-write, version metadata, guards against mixed spaces, cost estimate, and rollback.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A partial backfill left 18% of documents in the old space; those docs vanished from results with no error because cross-space cosine was low for all queries.

questions.contextHtml:
A contract-search team indexes 1,800-token clauses with intfloat/multilingual-e5-large using this code:

m = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-large")
vecs = m.encode([f"passage: {c}" for c in clauses], batch_size=64, normalize_embeddings=True)

Users report: searching a phrase that appears only in the second half of a clause never finds it, while searching the first sentence works perfectly. Recall on "first-half" test queries is 0.91, on "second-half" queries 0.18. No errors or warnings in logs. The model card says inputs longer than 512 tokens are truncated. Corpus: 400k clauses, token length median 1,100.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix. Include the trade-offs between possible fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase top-k" or "switch to a bigger model" without noticing the truncation; or "the model is bad at long text".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the model's max sequence length (card says 512)? Does m.max_seq_length show 512? What is the token length distribution (percent over 512)? Do users search with exact phrases or concepts? Can clauses be split semantically (headings, numbered sub-clauses)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add a lexical (BM25) leg so exact phrases from the tail still hit, via hybrid search, while the index is rebuilt.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) silent truncation at 512 tokens; (b) second-half content is boilerplate and uninformative; (c) mean pooling dilution; (d) wrong prefix. Truncation fits the asymmetric first-half/second-half result exactly.
  4. How to verify: print(m.max_seq_length); tokenize clauses with m.tokenizer and compute the percent over 512; embed the first 512 tokens vs full text and verify identical vectors; run the half-split queries.
  5. Root cause: Tokens beyond position 512 never enter the transformer, so the vector encodes only the head of each clause. Tail text is literally unsearchable by dense retrieval.
  6. Fix: Short-term: hybrid search. Long-term: chunk to ≤ ~400 tokens (leave room for the prefix) with overlap and parent-child mapping; or use a long-context embedding model (8k-token class models exist, e.g. OpenAI v3 at 8,192 per docs) knowing that one vector for 1,800 tokens blurs topics.
def chunks(tokens, size=400, overlap=60):
    step = size - overlap
    for i in range(0, max(1, len(tokens) - overlap), step):
        yield tokens[i:i+size]
  1. Prevention: At ingest, log the percent of chunks exceeding max_seq_length and fail the build above 1%; unit test that asserts token count ≤ limit.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Smaller chunks raise recall but multiply index size (1,800 tokens → ~5 chunks, so 400k → ~2M vectors; check memory per Q003). A long-context embedder keeps one vector per clause but dilutes specificity. I would not raise max_seq_length above what the model was trained for (position embeddings beyond training length degrade).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can you set m.max_seq_length = 2048? → For this model it exceeds trained positions (512 for XLM-R base positions); quality is unreliable; verify before trying.
  • Chunk overlap too high? → Duplicated hits and index bloat; dedupe by parent ID.
  • Mixed languages? → Token counts inflate for some languages; set limits in tokens, not characters (see the tokenization chunk).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A knowledge-base team blamed "poor semantic quality" for weeks; a 10-line script that counted tokens over the limit found 63% of documents were being cut.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Increases top-k or changes model blindly.
  • Hire: Identifies truncation, chunks to fit.
  • Strong hire: Quantifies impact, adds hybrid stopgap, ingest-time guard, discusses chunk-count/memory trade-off and long-context embedder limits.

questions.promptHtml: What are anisotropy and hubness in embedding spaces, and how do they affect retrieval quality?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who treat the vector space as ideal from those who know its geometry misbehaves.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Anisotropy means embeddings occupy a narrow cone instead of spreading across the sphere, so even unrelated texts have high cosine (a high baseline). Hubness means some vectors appear in the nearest-neighbor lists of a disproportionate number of queries, crowding out better answers. Both distort rankings and make absolute thresholds unreliable; mitigations are mean-centering/whitening, better-trained models, hybrid retrieval, and reranking.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Anisotropy: pretrained transformer representations share dominant directions (a large common mean vector and a few high-variance dims), so cosine between random pairs is far above 0. Contrastive fine-tuning reduces but does not eliminate this. Effect: score ranges compress (e.g. unrelated 0.65, related 0.80), so thresholds and "score margins" are tight and noisy.

Hubness: in high dimensions, distance concentration makes a few "hub" points frequent k-nearest neighbors of many others; a few "anti-hubs" never appear. Hubs are often generic, short, or boilerplate texts ("Contact support for more details"). They steal top-k slots.

Diagnostics:

  • k-occurrence N_k: for each doc, count how many queries/neighbors return it in top-k. Skew (high skewness of N_k) signals hubness.
  • Mean pairwise cosine of random samples (baseline).

Mitigations:

  1. Center vectors by subtracting the corpus mean, then re-normalize (cheap, often helps; re-test).
  2. Whitening/PCA (needs fit data; may drop useful dims).
  3. Cross-domain score normalization (CSLS-style: subtract each point's mean neighbor similarity). Verify applicability to your index type.
  4. Hybrid lexical + dense; cross-encoder rerank.
  5. Dedupe/remove boilerplate chunks at ingest.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
X = doc_vecs                                   # (N, d), normalized
mu = X.mean(0, keepdims=True)
Xc = X - mu; Xc /= np.linalg.norm(Xc, axis=1, keepdims=True)    # center + renormalize
idx = np.random.choice(len(X), 2000, replace=False)
print("baseline cos:", (X[idx] @ X[idx].T).mean(), "-> centered:", (Xc[idx] @ Xc[idx].T).mean())
# hubness: how often each doc shows up in others' top-10
nn = np.argsort(-(X[idx] @ X.T), axis=1)[:, 1:11]
counts = np.bincount(nn.ravel(), minlength=len(X))

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Centering docs but not queries with the same mean (must apply the same transform to both).
  • Applying whitening that removes dimensions carrying signal without re-evaluating.
  • Fixing hubs with thresholds instead of removing the boilerplate cause.
  • Computing the mean over a sample not representative of future data.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does higher dimension worsen hubness? → Distance concentration: pairwise distances become similar, so tiny asymmetries make some points disproportionately central.
  2. Does normalization fix anisotropy? → No; unit norm removes magnitude, not the shared direction.
  3. How do you know centering helped? → Recall@k and MRR on the eval set, plus reduced N_k skew; never trust the baseline-cosine number alone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cosine close to 1 means similar." Senior: knows baseline similarity is model-dependent, measures hubness, applies consistent centering, and relies on rerank/hybrid for residual error.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A FAQ search kept returning a generic "Contact us" chunk as top-3 for 22% of queries; deleting boilerplate chunks and mean-centering cut that to 1%.

questions.promptHtml: How do multilingual and multimodal embedding models work, and what pitfalls should you plan for?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Global products need cross-language search; image/text search is increasingly common.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Multilingual models train one encoder on many languages, often with parallel or translation-pair data, so equivalent sentences in different languages land near each other and cross-lingual retrieval works. Multimodal models like CLIP train two encoders (image and text) contrastively on image-caption pairs into a shared space. Pitfalls: uneven quality across languages, language bias in rankings, modality gap, and tokenization/length differences.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Multilingual: multilingual-e5-large is initialized from xlm-roberta-large, supports roughly 100 languages per its card (page metadata lists 94, so counts vary by source; verify), notes lower quality on low-resource languages, and requires query:/passage: prefixes for all languages. Cross-lingual retrieval (English query, Hindi doc) works because the space is aligned, but monolingual same-language pairs usually score higher than cross-lingual pairs, so a mixed corpus may favor documents in the query's language.

Multimodal (CLIP-style): image encoder + text encoder, contrastive loss on matched pairs. Both map into one space so text queries retrieve images. Known issue: modality gap, where image vectors and text vectors occupy separate regions of the sphere, so cross-modal cosine values are low in absolute terms and not comparable to text-text scores. Never mix text-text and text-image scores in one threshold.

text  --text encoder--\
                       >-- shared space, contrastive on (image, caption) pairs
image --image enc.----/

Practical points:

  • Token inflation in some languages shrinks the effective chunk size; set limits in tokens.
  • Language-ID the corpus and store a lang field for filters and eval slicing.
  • Evaluate per language; averages hide weak languages.
  • Code/identifiers: embedders trained on prose may struggle.
  • For long PDFs with figures, decide: embed page images directly (late-interaction vision-document models exist; verify maturity) or caption/OCR first.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
m = SentenceTransformer("intfloat/multilingual-e5-large")
q = m.encode(["query: refund policy"], normalize_embeddings=True)
d = m.encode(["passage: राशि वापसी नीति", "passage: refund policy"], normalize_embeddings=True)
print(q @ d.T)   # compare cross-lingual vs same-language score; expect same-language higher

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming parity across languages and shipping with English-only eval.
  • One global threshold across languages.
  • Mixing modalities' scores in one ranking without calibration.
  • Forgetting prefixes for non-English text.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. English-only corpus, multilingual queries? → Works with a multilingual model; or translate queries; evaluate both.
  2. Translate-then-embed vs multilingual embed? → Translation adds latency/cost/errors but can use a stronger English model; test both on labeled data.
  3. How to handle low-resource languages? → Fine-tune with in-language pairs, hybrid lexical retrieval, or per-language fallback.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use a multilingual model." Senior: slices evals per language, handles cross-language bias and modality gap, per-language thresholds, token-based limits.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An e-commerce search with a single 0.75 threshold surfaced results for English and nothing for Thai because Thai scores sat lower on the same model; per-language calibration fixed it.

questions.contextHtml: A product search service has 60M product-description chunks embedded with an MRL-capable 1024-dim model (float32), served from pgvector-like infrastructure with HNSW. RAM bill: 60M × 1024 × 4 B = 245.8 GB of raw vectors; with graph overhead and 2 replicas the team provisions ~900 GB. Finance asks for a 60% reduction. An engineer ships "truncate to 256 dims" by slicing vec[:256] in the indexer and the query service, storing without renormalization, and keeping the index on inner product. Next day: recall@10 on the golden set goes from 0.88 to 0.79, and the long-description products dominate results. Latency improved 35%.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, and how would you get the savings without the quality loss?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Truncation always loses quality; revert." It does not separate the avoidable bug (renormalization) from the real trade-off, and does not use rescoring or quantization.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the model actually Matryoshka-trained at 256 (check the card)? Is the index IP, cosine, or L2? What recall target do we need, and what latency? Are the full vectors still available in cold storage? What is the long-tail query mix?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll the query side to cosine scoring (or renormalize both) if full vectors exist; otherwise renormalize prefix vectors from the stored ones in a batch job and swap.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) missing renormalization: a 256-prefix of a unit vector has norm <1 and varies by document, so IP is norm-biased (explains long-description domination); (b) 256 is below the model's usable prefix sizes; (c) thresholds/score cutoffs not recalibrated; (d) HNSW params tuned for 1024-dim not re-tuned.
  4. How to verify: Compute the norm of 256-prefixes (mean/std); correlate norm with rank position; recompute recall@10 with renormalized prefixes offline on the golden set at 128/256/512 dims; test cosine vs IP.
  5. Root cause: ||v[:256]|| < 1, differing per doc, so the dot product mixes angle with norm; plus some real information loss at 256d.
  6. Fix: Renormalize, then measure the curve. Then use two-stage retrieval: HNSW over 256d (int8 if supported) for top-200, rescore with full 1024d vectors stored on SSD or in a cheaper tier.
def to256(v):  # v: (n, 1024) unit vectors
    t = v[:, :256]
    return t / np.linalg.norm(t, axis=1, keepdims=True)
# memory: 60M*256*4 = 61.4 GB (4x less); int8: 15.4 GB (16x less)
  1. Prevention: Golden-set gate in CI for any index change; assert norms; record dims, quantization and model ID in index metadata.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Rescoring adds a disk/RAM read for 200 vectors per query (+ a few ms). Binary quantization saves most but loses precision; only with rescoring. I would not ship dimension cuts without the eval gate, nor chase the last 1 point of recall at 2x cost if the product tolerance is wider.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The model is not MRL-trained → Truncation is off the table; use int8/PQ with rescoring, or switch to an MRL model.
  • Recall drops only on rare queries → Segment the eval by query frequency; maybe route tail queries to the full index.
  • Need 64d for an on-device cache? → Usually only with a distilled or MRL model; test.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team cut dimensions to meet a budget deadline, forgot normalization, and the first sign was a support ticket about "the same giant product always at the top". The golden-set gate was added the same week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Reverts without diagnosis.
  • Hire: Finds missing renormalization, shows memory math.
  • Strong hire: Two-stage rescoring with quantization plan, metadata/versioning, eval gate, and cost numbers.

questions.contextHtml: Your vendor announces that embed-v2 is deprecated in 90 days. You have 120M chunks (avg 280 tokens), a 1,536-dim index serving 400 QPS peak, p95 SLA of 120 ms, and uptime commitments. The new model embed-v3 has a rate limit of 4M tokens/minute (illustrative) and costs $0.10 per 1M tokens (illustrative; check actual). Total tokens: 120M × 280 = 33.6B. Product wants the new model's better quality ASAP, and also wants "zero downtime". The index team says double the cluster for the migration is too expensive. Some documents change daily (~0.5M/day).
questions.promptHtml: Plan the migration end to end, with numbers.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Re-embed everything overnight and switch." Ignores rate limits (33.6B / 4M per minute = 8,400 minutes = 5.8 days), cost ($3,360), live writes, and rollback.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 90-day deadline hard, and what happens after (error or fallback)? Can we get higher rate limits or batch API pricing? Is raw text stored? Which collections matter most (prioritize hot content)? What is the quality gate to cut over?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin the current model ID, add a metadata field embed_model, and ensure the query service refuses mismatches. No behavior change yet.
  3. Hypotheses (risks), ranked: (a) backfill throughput misestimated; (b) mixed-space queries during partial backfill; (c) new model needs different prefixes/dimension/threshold; (d) index memory doubling during dual-run; (e) quality regressions on a segment.
  4. How I'd verify: Benchmark embed-v3 on the golden set per segment (language, length); sample 1M chunks to measure true tokens and throughput; load-test the dual index at 1.5x QPS; compute score distributions for threshold re-calibration.
  5. Root cause (of the problem): Vector spaces are model-specific, so vendor lifecycle forces a full re-embed; the design must make that routine.
  6. Fix (plan):
    • Build index_v3 in a separate namespace/cluster, shard-by-shard. Backfill order: hot/most-queried collections first.
    • Throughput: 33.6B tokens at 4M TPM ≈ 5.8 days continuous; ask for a batch endpoint or higher limits; budget ~$3.4k at the illustrative price. Make the job idempotent (chunk_id + model_id key), checkpointed, and retry with backoff.
    • Dual-write: new/changed docs go to both indexes (0.5M/day is small).
    • Cut-over per collection via alias: query path embeds with both models in shadow for 1 week, logging overlap@10 and eval metrics; canary 5% → 25% → 100%.
    • Memory: if dimensions differ, use MRL or int8 for v3 to keep the footprint flat; delete v2 shards progressively after each collection cuts over.
    • Recalibrate thresholds from labeled pairs before cut-over (Q010).
    • Rollback: keep v2 for 14 days at least.
  7. Prevention: Make "re-embed everything" a tested runbook; store raw text; metadata for model/chunker/prefix versions; quarterly drill with a 1% sample.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not an all-at-once switch; not mixing spaces in one index; not trying query-time vector translation for the main path; not skipping the shadow period to hit a date.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Rate limit is 10x lower → Prioritize hot data, partial migration with hybrid lexical fallback for the cold tail, or self-host an open model for the bulk.
  • Quality is worse for Hindi → Segment-level cutover; keep v2 for that segment until the deadline, escalate to the vendor or fine-tune.
  • Docs change during backfill → Dual-write with versioned chunk IDs; reconcile by updated_at.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team planned a weekend migration; the first dry run showed the rate limit alone needed a week. Splitting into hot-first batches kept the deadline.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Big-bang re-embed.
  • Hire: Blue/green with dual-write and rollback, notices rate limit.
  • Strong hire: Quantified throughput/cost, shadow evaluation, per-segment cutover, memory plan, threshold recalibration, repeatable runbook.

questions.contextHtml: A support assistant uses a semantic cache: if cosine(new_query, cached_query) ≥ 0.88, return the cached answer. It has run for 6 months with a 31% hit rate and "no complaints". Last Tuesday the team upgraded the embedding model (new vendor version, same dimension, vectors normalized) and re-embedded the cache keys. Hit rate jumped to 58%, p95 latency dropped, and cost fell, so the dashboard looked great. Three days later: a customer received instructions for "downgrading a plan" when asking about "upgrading a plan"; 11 similar tickets follow. Sample logged pairs: ("how to upgrade my plan", "how to downgrade my plan") scored 0.91.
questions.promptHtml: Write the post-incident review: causes, detection gaps, and corrective actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Raise the threshold to 0.95." Ignores that scores are model-specific, that hit rate is a vanity metric, and that antonyms are a known embedding weakness.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
