1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the threshold re-calibrated for the new model? Is there any answer-validation step? What is the cost of a wrong cached answer per intent type? Do we have labeled query pairs (same vs different intent)? Are cached answers context-dependent (account, plan)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable the cache for intent categories with high-stakes or negation/contrast pairs, or raise the threshold to a conservative value temporarily and flush entries created since the upgrade; add a "shadow mode" log.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the new model compresses the score range so 0.88 is now looser (hit rate doubled is the tell); (b) embeddings cannot distinguish antonyms/negation reliably; (c) the cache ignores user context; (d) threshold tests only measured hit rate.
  4. How to verify: Replay 20k logged queries against old and new models; label 500 pairs (same intent / different intent) including hard negatives; plot score distributions; compute precision at 0.88 for each model.
  5. Root cause: A threshold tuned on the old model was carried over. The score scale changed (anisotropy differs per model), pushing "contrastive" pairs above the cutoff. Underlying weakness: dense vectors encode topic more than polarity.
  6. Fix: Re-calibrate per model on hard-negative pairs to target precision ≥ 0.99 for auto-serve. Add verification: a cross-encoder or small LLM check ("do these queries ask the same thing?") on candidate hits, or intent classification before caching. Key the cache on context (tenant, plan, locale).
hit = best.score >= T_CAL[model_id]            # per-model calibrated threshold
if hit and not same_intent(query, best.query): hit = False   # verifier; cross-encoder or LLM
  1. Prevention: Threshold stored as config tied to model ID; any model change triggers calibration eval in CI; monitor wrong-answer proxies (thumbs-down rate on cache hits vs misses, re-ask rate), not just hit rate; hard-negative test set (upgrade/downgrade, enable/disable, with/without).
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: A verifier adds 20-80 ms (illustrative) and cost, eroding savings; accept for high-risk intents, skip for FAQ-grade. I would not celebrate hit rate, nor set one global threshold.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership wants hit rate back at 50% → Show precision/recall curve; trade by intent tier; use verification to regain hits safely.
  • Cache entries created under the old model remain → Tag by model ID and purge on change.
  • Multilingual queries → Calibrate per language.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "great week" dashboard turned into a trust incident because success was defined by hit rate; the postmortem added a wrong-hit budget as a launch gate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Just raise the threshold.
  • Hire: Ties incident to model upgrade and recalibrates.
  • Strong hire: Hard-negative set, verifier, context keys, metrics on harm not hit rate, process gate on model swaps.

questions.promptHtml: Is cosine similarity of learned embeddings always meaningful? What are its limits, and is cosine distance a metric?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes depth beyond "use cosine"; research-aware engineers stand out.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cosine is a sensible default when the model was trained for it, but it is not guaranteed meaningful for arbitrary learned embeddings. Steck et al. (2024) show that for matrix-factorization-style models trained with regularization, cosine can be made arbitrary by rescaling latent dimensions while the dot products stay fixed. Practically: use the metric the model was trained with and validate with retrieval evals. Also, 1 - cosine violates the triangle inequality, so it is not a true metric; angular distance is.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The paper (arXiv 2403.05440): in models like linear matrix factorization, a diagonal rescaling of the latent dimensions leaves the dot products of predictions unchanged but alters the cosine between embeddings, so cosine reflects an arbitrary training artifact (regularization), not an intrinsic similarity. Takeaway for LLM embeddings: contrastively trained text models optimize cosine (or normalized dot) directly with a temperature, so cosine is meaningful for them, but the lesson stands: similarity is defined by the loss, and a metric the model never optimized may mislead.

Triangle inequality: cosine distance d = 1 - cos. Counter-example with angles: A,B at 0° and 90°, C at 45°. d(A,B)=1, d(A,C)=1-0.7071=0.2929, d(C,B)=0.2929; sum 0.5858 < 1, so d(A,B) > d(A,C)+d(C,B). Violated. Angular distance θ = arccos(cos) satisfies it (45+45 ≥ 90). Consequences: metric-tree pruning (e.g. ball trees) assumes triangle inequality, so use normalized vectors + L2 (a true metric whose ranking equals cosine's) when an algorithm needs a metric.

Other limits: scores aren't probabilities (Q010), they depend on text length, they say nothing about factual correctness, and high cosine ≠ answers the question (topical vs answer-bearing).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
A, B, C = np.array([1,0.]), np.array([0,1.]), np.array([1,1.])/np.sqrt(2)
cd = lambda x, y: 1 - x @ y
print(cd(A,B), cd(A,C) + cd(C,B))     # 1.0 vs 0.586 -> triangle inequality violated
ang = lambda x, y: np.arccos(np.clip(x @ y, -1, 1))
print(ang(A,B), ang(A,C) + ang(C,B))  # 1.571 vs 1.571 -> holds (equal here)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using cosine distance in a metric-assuming data structure.
  • Treating high cosine as "answers the question".
  • Applying the paper's matrix-factorization result directly to contrastive text encoders.
  • Mixing metrics between training, indexing, and thresholding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does normalized L2 equal cosine ranking? → ||a-b||² = 2-2cos for unit vectors (Q002).
  2. When is raw dot product better? → When norm encodes a deliberate signal (popularity) and the model was trained on dot.
  3. Alternatives to a single-vector cosine? → Late-interaction (token-level MaxSim) and cross-encoders for finer matching.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cosine measures semantic similarity." Senior: similarity is loss-defined, validates empirically, knows the triangle-inequality and arbitrariness caveats, and uses the trained metric.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team used a ball-tree library with 1 - cosine for dedup and got inconsistent clusters; switching to normalized L2 made results consistent.

questions.contextHtml: An internal doc-search tool runs brute-force cosine in NumPy on a single 32 GB box: 2M chunks × 768d float32 = 6.1 GB, p95 = 85 ms at 20 QPS. Acquisition of a second company will take the corpus to 25M chunks and traffic to 200 QPS. A quick extrapolation says brute force will be roughly 12x slower per query (about 1 s), and memory will be 76.8 GB. The team proposes "just add GPUs" or "move to a managed vector DB, whichever is cheapest".
questions.promptHtml: How do you scale this, and what do you measure before committing?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a product by name, never mentions recall, memory math, or index parameters; or says "HNSW, done".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Recall target and latency SLO? Filters per tenant/ACL (they change index choice)? Update rate and deletions? Budget and ops skill? Can chunks be quantized or truncated (is the model MRL)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed yet; this is capacity planning. Keep the current service and build the new path beside it with a recall comparison against brute force on a sample.
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked: (a) HNSW with float32: 25M × 768 × 4 = 76.8 GB plus links, which needs a big-RAM node; (b) HNSW with int8 scalar quantization (~19 GB vectors) plus rescoring; (c) IVF-PQ for tight memory with lower recall; (d) sharding across nodes for QPS; (e) GPU brute force: viable at this size but costs more per QPS than CPU ANN.
  4. How I'd verify: Build each on a 2M sample, then at 25M; measure recall@10 vs exact (ground truth from brute force on 1k queries), p50/p95/p99, build time, RAM, and QPS per core; test with real filters.
  5. Root cause (of the problem): Brute force is O(N·d) per query; N grew 12.5x.
  6. Fix: HNSW (M≈16-32, tuned efSearch) with scalar quantization and rescoring from full vectors on disk, sharded to 2-3 replicas for 200 QPS; target recall@10 ≥ 0.95 vs exact. Quick estimate: 200 QPS × ~5 ms/query ≈ 1 core-second per second per replica, so a few cores per replica leave headroom.
# recall guard used in CI for every index config change
def recall(approx_ids, exact_ids): return np.mean([len(set(a) & set(e)) / len(e) for a, e in zip(approx_ids, exact_ids)])
assert recall(a, e) >= 0.95
  1. Prevention: Track recall (sampled shadow brute force nightly) and p99; alert on drift after bulk ingests; capacity model by vector count.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Higher ef = more recall, more latency. Quantization saves RAM at a small recall cost, recovered by rescoring. I would not pick a vendor before measuring recall on my data, nor let managed-service defaults stand unmeasured.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Multi-tenant with strict ACL filters → Filtered search can hurt HNSW recall (Q021); consider per-tenant partitions or pre-filter strategies.
  • Corpus hits 500M → IVF-PQ or disk-based ANN, sharded; accept lower recall with rescoring.
  • Daily bulk reindex → Build into a new index and swap; avoid in-place heavy churn.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "10x" migration passed latency tests but nobody measured recall; a sampled brute-force audit later showed 0.78 recall@10 from default ef settings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Names a product/GPUs only.
  • Hire: Does memory math, picks ANN, mentions recall.
  • Strong hire: Compares options with measured recall/latency/RAM, quantization plus rescoring, filter and update considerations.

questions.contextHtml: A stakeholder says: "We need semantic search over our contracts in English, German, and Japanese. Make it accurate. Use the best embedding model." Corpus: 300k contracts, average 12 pages, sensitive client data; deadline in 6 weeks; two ML engineers; no labeled queries; legal team available 2 hours/week. Budget is "reasonable".
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into a decision and a plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use the top of the MTEB leaderboard." No requirements gathering, no eval, ignores privacy, language slices, and length.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "accurate" mean (find the clause, find the contract, find precedent)? Is cross-language querying needed (German query, English doc)? Can data leave our cloud (API vs self-host)? Query volume and latency? What is the cost of a missed clause vs a wrong hit? Exact-term needs (clause numbers, party names) pointing to hybrid search?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first week I produce a one-page spec with success metrics (recall@10 ≥ X on legal-labeled queries, p95 < 300 ms) and constraints, agreed with the stakeholder.
  3. Hypotheses (candidate approaches), ranked: (a) a multilingual open model self-hosted (privacy-safe), (b) a hosted API model under a data-processing agreement, (c) hybrid BM25 + dense, (d) translation pipeline (usually worse for legal nuance).
  4. How I'd verify: Build ~150 queries with the legal team (use LLM-generated drafts from sampled clauses, human-verified in 2 hours/week), sliced by language and cross-language; run 3 candidates (e.g. an open multilingual model, a hosted model, plus BM25 baseline) and compare recall@10/MRR per slice, latency, cost, and token limits (clauses may exceed 512 tokens).
  5. Root cause (of the ambiguity): "Best" is undefined; model quality is task- and language-specific.
  6. Fix (plan): Weeks 1: spec + eval set. Week 2-3: candidates + chunking by clause/heading. Week 4: hybrid + rerank if needed. Week 5: shadow pilot with users. Week 6: ship with monitoring and golden-set regression.
slices = {"en": q_en, "de": q_de, "ja": q_ja, "de->en": q_de_en}
for name, qs in slices.items(): print(name, evaluate(retriever, qs))
  1. Prevention: Keep the eval set versioned; track per-language metrics; log failed searches for the next labeling round.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Self-host costs ops but keeps data in; API is faster to ship but needs legal sign-off. I would not choose on MTEB average, translate everything by default, or ship without a Japanese-specific eval.

sections.html:
• Legal can't give labeling time → LLM-generated queries from clauses plus a 30-query human audit; flag the weaker evidence.
  • Stakeholder insists on one specific vendor → Include it as a candidate and let the numbers speak.
  • Mixed-language contracts → Chunk-level language ID and per-language checks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team skipped scoping and built for conceptual search; users actually pasted clause numbers and defined terms, which dense retrieval missed until BM25 was added.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks a model immediately.
  • Hire: Asks for success criteria and builds an eval set.
  • Strong hire: Language-sliced eval, privacy-driven hosting decision, hybrid search, timeline with checkpoints.

questions.contextHtml: A multi-tenant RAG product with 80M chunks in one HNSW index (M=16, efSearch=64) supports a tenant_id filter applied after ANN retrieval ("post-filter"). Median tenant owns 0.01% of vectors (8k chunks); the largest owns 12%. Support tickets: "search returns nothing" for small tenants; for some it returns 1-2 results while the tenant has hundreds of relevant docs. Logs: ann.candidates=64 filtered_out=63 returned=1. Overall recall@10 on the global golden set is 0.93 and p95 latency is a healthy 22 ms. A recent change: the team deleted 15M stale vectors via tombstones last week.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose, mitigate, and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "The embeddings for small tenants are bad" or "increase top-k to 1000 globally" with no thought about selectivity, latency, or tombstones.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the filter applied before, during, or after ANN search? What does the engine do for highly selective filters? What is the tombstone ratio and have we compacted? Are tenants isolated for compliance (which hints at partitioning anyway)? Per-tenant recall requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: For tenants flagged small, route to exact brute-force over their own vectors (8k × d is trivial) or a filtered flat scan; this restores results immediately.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) post-filtering with low selectivity: only 64 candidates, the chance that any belong to a 0.01% tenant is tiny; (b) filter-aware traversal disabled or degraded by graph connectivity; (c) tombstones: deleted nodes still sit in the graph, wasting candidates and weakening connectivity until compaction; (d) per-tenant embedding quality (red herring: logs show candidates were filtered, not irrelevant).
  4. How to verify: Compute expected survivors: 64 × 0.0001 ≈ 0.0064 per query; measure the fraction of queries returning < k per tenant size; compare to brute-force-in-tenant ground truth; check index stats for deleted count; test with filtered-search mode and higher ef.
  5. Root cause: Post-filtering plus extremely selective filters yields too few survivors; global recall hides per-tenant failure because large tenants dominate the average. Tombstones worsen graph search quality.
  6. Fix: Short-term: exact search for small tenants; compact/rebuild after mass deletions. Long-term: partition by tenant (collection/namespace/partition key per tenant tier), or use an engine with filter-aware HNSW traversal; adapt ef to filter selectivity; large tenants keep a shared ANN index.
def search(tenant, q, k=10):
    n = tenant_count[tenant]
    if n <= 50_000:        # exact on small tenants: cheap and complete
        return flat_scan(tenant_vectors(tenant), q, k)
    return hnsw.search(q, k, filter={"tenant_id": tenant}, ef=max(64, int(k / selectivity(tenant))))
  1. Prevention: Report recall and zero/low-result rate per tenant-size bucket; alert on returned < k; schedule compaction when the deleted fraction passes a threshold (e.g. 10-20%, tune per engine); filter-selectivity test in CI.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Per-tenant indexes multiply object count and overhead; hybrid tiering balances this. Raising ef globally costs latency for everyone. I would not blame embeddings or lower k expectations.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Pre-filter instead? → Exact within the filtered set is fine for small sets; for mid-size sets use filter-aware ANN; pure pre-filter on a graph can disconnect it.
  • Tenant ACLs per user (not per tenant) → Highly selective, dynamic filters; consider re-ranking post-retrieval with over-fetch plus access checks, or per-ACL partitions.
  • Deletion for compliance (must be erased) → Tombstones are insufficient; rebuild/compact to physically remove, and document the SLA.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A dashboard showed 0.93 global recall for months while the smallest 5% of customers had effectively no search; bucketing the metric by tenant size exposed it in a day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Blames embeddings or raises top-k globally.
  • Hire: Identifies post-filter selectivity, uses exact or partitioned search for small tenants.
  • Strong hire: Does the survivor math, adds tombstone/compaction analysis, per-bucket metrics, and a tiered architecture.

questions.promptHtml: How do you evaluate an embedding model or an index change, and what are the limits of public benchmarks like MTEB?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The senior skill is knowing quality is measured, not assumed; also tests metric literacy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I evaluate the retrieval task end to end on a labeled set drawn from real queries: recall@k, MRR, and nDCG, sliced by language, query type, and document length, and compare against brute-force ground truth to separate model error from ANN error. Public benchmarks like MTEB help shortlist but average across tasks, can be contaminated or tuned for, and rarely match my domain, so they never replace my own eval.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two error sources:

  1. Model error: relevant doc not near the query in embedding space. Measured by exact (brute-force) search recall against labels.
  2. ANN error: index misses true neighbors. Measured by approximate vs exact top-k overlap. Keeping them separate prevents tuning the wrong thing.

Metrics:

  • recall@k: fraction of relevant docs found in top-k (matters when a downstream LLM/reranker consumes top-k).
  • MRR: 1/rank of the first relevant doc (one right answer).
  • nDCG@k: graded relevance with position discount. Tiny worked example: relevant doc at rank 3 in a query: recall@5 = 1, MRR = 1/3 ≈ 0.33; at rank 1: MRR 1.

Building the set: sample real queries (or LLM-generate from chunks, then human-verify); hard negatives matter. Beware synthetic queries that copy chunk wording (inflates lexical overlap).

Limits of MTEB: averaged scores hide per-task variance; leaderboard entries can be trained on benchmark-adjacent data (check for self-reported results; verify methodology); task mix differs from your retrieval; English-heavy tasks unless using multilingual subsets. OpenAI's docs cite MTEB figures (3-small 62.3%, 3-large 64.6%); treat as indicative, not decisive.

Operational metrics: embed latency, index RAM, cost per 1M tokens, and downstream answer quality (end-to-end RAG eval belongs to the RAG/eval chunks).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import numpy as np
def mrr(ranked, rel): 
    for i, d in enumerate(ranked, 1):
        if d in rel: return 1 / i
    return 0.0
def ndcg_at_k(ranked, gains, k=10):      # gains: dict doc_id -> graded relevance
    dcg = sum(gains.get(d, 0) / np.log2(i + 2) for i, d in enumerate(ranked[:k]))
    ideal = sorted(gains.values(), reverse=True)[:k]
    idcg = sum(g / np.log2(i + 2) for i, g in enumerate(ideal))
    return dcg / idcg if idcg else 0.0

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting only a global average.
  • Evaluating with the same data used to tune thresholds or fine-tune.
  • Eval queries derived from the chunk text, rewarding lexical overlap.
  • Changing chunking and model in one experiment, so the cause is unknowable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How big should the eval set be? → Enough that the confidence interval on the difference is below the effect you care about; 100-300 queries is a practical start; bootstrap the difference.
  2. How do you detect regressions over time? → Fixed golden set in CI plus sampled production queries with periodic relabeling.
  3. recall@k vs downstream answer quality? → Recall is necessary, not sufficient; context packing, reranking, and generation also matter (see the RAG and evals chunks).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "check MTEB and try a few queries." Senior: separates model and ANN error, uses sliced metrics with confidence intervals, controls one variable at a time, and gates changes in CI.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team swapped to a higher-MTEB model and saw support deflection fall; sliced eval showed gains on English narrative text but regressions on short product-code queries, which dominated traffic.
